findings.paper_title: Financial Performance 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital programme delivered at only 83% with £2.1m carried forward to next year
findings.detail: Breckland spent only 83% of its planned capital budget in 2025-26, with £2.1m of capital funding carried forward to 2026-27. The reasons for individual projects' underperformance are detailed in Appendix B but not in this summary.
findings.matters: Capital delivery shortfalls can indicate slippage in project delivery capability or changes in priorities; £2.1m carried forward is material and indicates potential delays in schemes expected to deliver benefits.
findings.figures: £2.1m carried forward; 83% spend rate
findings.quote: The capital programme was 83% spent against budget, with requests to carry forward £2.1m of unused capital funding.

findings.paper_title: Financial Performance 2025-26
findings.headline: Council tax collection ended below budget due to VOA delays, reduced new homes, and cost of living impacts
findings.detail: Council tax collection in 2025-26 was under budget. Three factors contributed: delays in the Valuation Office Agency rating new properties, a smaller than anticipated increase in new homes, and cost of living impacts affecting residents' ability to pay.
findings.matters: Council tax is the primary revenue source; under-collection signals both external pressures (development slowdown) and resident payment difficulty, both of which reduce revenue security for the council and increase default risk.
findings.figures: Collection ended 'under budget' but no specific shortfall figure provided
findings.quote: Council Tax collection remains under budget for the year due to a range of reasons including delays in the VOA rating new properties, reduced increase in new homes and the cost of living impacts.

findings.paper_title: Financial Performance 2025-26
findings.headline: A budgeting error within the PFI scheme resulted in the budget being set incorrectly for the year
findings.detail: The council made an error in calculating the budget for a PFI (Private Finance Initiative) scheme for 2025-26, which led to above-budget spend. No detail is provided on the scale of the error, which PFI scheme was affected, or how the error was discovered.
findings.matters: PFI schemes are long-term contractual commitments with fixed costs; budgeting errors on these indicate control weaknesses in how major spending lines are forecast and monitored.
findings.figures: No specific figure for the error disclosed; details are in Appendix A
findings.quote: A budgeting error within the PFI scheme resulted in the budget being set incorrectly for the year

findings.paper_title: Financial Performance 2025-26
findings.headline: Bad debt and loan impairments for Breckland Bridge led to large above-budget spend
findings.detail: The council made a significant provision for bad debt and possible loan impairments related to Breckland Bridge during 2025-26, listed as a major area of above-budget spend. The report does not detail what Breckland Bridge is, the scale of the impairment, or whether further provisions may be needed.
findings.matters: Loan impairments indicate that previous lending or investment decisions are underperforming, directly affecting cash reserves and raising questions about investment governance and whether future cash flows are at risk.
findings.figures: Described as 'large overspend' but no specific figure disclosed in this document; details are in Appendix A
findings.quote: A provision for bad debt and a provision for possible loan impairments for Breckland Bridge have led to a large overspend in this financial year

findings.paper_title: Annual report on the Treasury Management service and actual Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: Economic forecast inverted mid-year: rate cuts anticipated in strategy became rate rises expected by March 2026, driven by inflation and Middle East conflict.
findings.detail: The council's treasury strategy (approved December 2024) forecast gradual interest rate reductions through 2025-26. By April 2026, market expectations reversed to rate rises to 4–4.25% from 3.75%. The council cites Middle East conflict as driving inflation concerns, with CPI expected to breach 4.5% later in 2026. This materially raises future borrowing costs.
findings.matters: A rise in long-term borrowing rates (5-year PWLB now 4.50% vs 4.40% forecast) increases the cost of any future capital schemes and reduces the council's ability to afford them.
findings.figures: Bank Rate 3.75%; market now expects 4–4.25%; CPI forecast >4.5%
findings.quote: At the start of April 2026, the market expected Bank Rate to increase over the coming months to 4% or 4.25%, from 3.75%

findings.paper_title: Annual report on the Treasury Management service and actual Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: Unfunded capital expenditure jumped 65% to £3.2m, with Capital Financing Requirement rising £2m.
findings.detail: Unfinanced capital spend grew from £1.94m to £3.2m, one of the largest year-on-year moves in the report. The Capital Financing Requirement (the underlying borrowing need) rose from £4.5m to £6.5m. The council is managing this through underborrowing (using cash reserves), but accumulating capital pressure will eventually force borrowing.
findings.matters: Growing capital deficits signal increasing pressure on reserves and a future borrowing need; if sustained, this erodes debt capacity and headroom.
findings.figures: Unfinanced capital expenditure: £1,936k → £3,201k; CFR: £4,516k → £6,520k
findings.quote: Unfinanced Capital Expenditure 1,936 2,709 3,201

findings.paper_title: Annual report on the Treasury Management service and actual Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: Non-treasury investments (third-party loans) nearly doubled from £2.77m to £5.13m, now 15% of all investments.
findings.detail: The council's loans to third parties rose 85% year-on-year, growing from 8.2% to 15.1% of total investments. These are commercial/service delivery loans, not treasury investments, and carry higher default risk than treasury-rated counterparties. This represents a material shift in risk profile.
findings.matters: Rapid growth in concentrated loans to third parties signals rising exposure to single counterparties and commercial losses; deterioration of reserve quality if any third party defaults.
findings.figures: Third party loans £2,771k → £5,133k; share of total: 8.2% → 15.1%
findings.quote: Third party loans 2,771 5,133

findings.paper_title: Annual report on the Treasury Management service and actual Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: Breckland Bridge loans exceeded the council's £5m treasury limit in March 2026 by £133k—a breach of internal controls.
findings.detail: The council's loans to Breckland Bridge, a service company, breached the approved £5m limit during March 2026. The council recovers the position by adjusting for expected impairment of the Colkirk scheme, but the breach itself represents a failure of treasury control and monitoring.
findings.matters: Breaches of internal treasury limits expose gaps in financial controls and increase risk of losses or further covenant breaches not being caught.
findings.figures: £133k excess; £5m limit
findings.quote: As a result of an error, the total amount of loans provided to Breckland Bridge exceeded the £5m limit during March 2026 by £133k.

findings.paper_title: 25.BC.LG Auditors Annual Report (AAR) 24-25 - final
findings.headline: Council is behind trajectory for rebuilding audit assurance and will likely remain disclaimed through 2025/26.
findings.detail: The auditor states the council is behind the NAO's expected timescale for recovering from prior disclaimer. Because all procedures could not be completed in 2024/25, the auditor anticipates 2025/26 financial statements will also be disclaimed, with full recovery not expected until 2026/27 at earliest.
findings.matters: Multiple years of unaudited accounts means prolonged inability to independently verify financial position and compliance with accounting standards—extending audit uncertainty across the medium term.
findings.figures: Expected: disclaimer 2024/25, likely disclaimer 2025/26, possible qualified opinion 2026/27
findings.quote: The Council is currently behind the illustrative timescale for the process of re-building assurance, because not all audit procedures were completed during either 2023/24 or 2024/25. The opinion for 2024/25 has been disclaimed.

findings.paper_title: 25.BC.LG Auditors Annual Report (AAR) 24-25 - final
findings.headline: Two urgent internal audit recommendations remain overdue: procurement governance and private sector housing controls.
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit reported three overdue agreed actions for 2024/25, including two marked urgent. One concerns strengthening procurement governance and regulatory adherence; the other involves strengthening oversight and controls in private sector housing. Overdue recommendations indicate control gaps are not being remediated.
findings.matters: Overdue internal audit actions signal identified control weaknesses are not being addressed, particularly concerning for procurement (expenditure controls) and housing (potential revenue or capital commitments).
findings.figures: Three overdue actions: two urgent, one routine
findings.quote: The Head of Internal Audit noted that there are three agreed actions that are overdue in 2024/25, where two recommendations are urgent and one routine. The two overdue urgent recommendations relate to Contract and Procurement and Private Sector Housing.

findings.paper_title: 25.BC.LG Auditors Annual Report (AAR) 24-25 - final
findings.headline: Pension liability required £21.338 million restatement during audit process.
findings.detail: The draft accounts undervalued the pension liability because they did not correctly apply the asset ceiling impact. The actuary provided updated information during audit, requiring a £21.338 million adjustment to pension liability and reserves in the final accounts.
findings.matters: This large restatement indicates the council's initial financial reporting process failed to properly account for a major liability, suggesting accounting knowledge gaps or process failures.
findings.figures: £21.338 million increase to Pension Liability
findings.quote: Audit difference of £21.338 million in relation to an increase in the valuation of Pension Liability due to the impact of the asset ceiling. The adjustment was made due to updated information provided by the Actuary after the draft Statement of Accounts was prepared.

findings.paper_title: 25.BC.LG Auditors Annual Report (AAR) 24-25 - final
findings.headline: The Accountancy Manager and Deputy Section 151 Officer left the council just before year-end audit.
findings.detail: These departures forced the council to engage temporary resources and caused loss of institutional knowledge. The auditor explicitly notes this contributed to delays in providing evidence and responses during the audit.
findings.matters: The Section 151 Officer is chief financial officer. Turnover of the deputy and Accountancy Manager during the peak audit season indicates possible instability in financial leadership.
findings.figures: Departures: just before year-end audit, March 2025
findings.quote: The Accountancy Manager and Deputy Section 151 Officer left the Council just before the year-end audit. The loss of knowledge contributed to delays during the audit.

findings.paper_title: 25.BC.LG Auditors Annual Report (AAR) 24-25 - final
findings.headline: Auditor unable to complete procedures for Property, Plant & Equipment, Investment Properties, IFRS 16 Leases, and Reserves.
findings.detail: These represent the largest items on most councils' balance sheets. Absence of audit procedures over these means there is no independent verification of their values or existence. These incomplete procedures contributed to the disclaimer opinion.
findings.matters: Without audited balance sheet values, the true asset position and borrowing capacity cannot be verified, creating significant uncertainty around financial position.
findings.figures: Unable to complete planned procedures for major balance sheet categories
findings.quote: We have been unable to complete all planned 2024/25 procedures for Balance Sheet - Property, Plant and Equipment, Balance Sheet - Investment Property, Balance Sheet - IFRS16 Lease; Balance Sheet – Reserves.

findings.paper_title: 25.BC.LG Auditors Annual Report (AAR) 24-25 - final
findings.headline: Auditor issued disclaimer of opinion on 2024/25 financial statements, meaning the council's accounts are not assured.
findings.detail: The auditor could not obtain sufficient evidence to provide assurance that the 2024/25 financial statements are free from material and pervasive misstatement. This follows a similar disclaimer on 2023/24. The disclaimer was issued because of pervasive gaps in assurance over opening balances, comparators, and in-year movements, particularly Property, Plant & Equipment valuation.
findings.matters: A lender typically requires audited financial statements before making lending decisions. A disclaimer means the council's actual financial position cannot be independently verified.
findings.figures: Disclaimer issued 17 February 2026
findings.quote: We are unable to conclude that the 2024/25 financial statements are free from material and pervasive misstatement. We therefore issued a disclaimer of opinion on the 2024/25 Statement of Accounts on 17 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Q1 Strategic risk report
findings.headline: Waste service rollout in late September 2026 is explicitly dependent on delivery of waste vehicles
findings.detail: The waste strategy risk has been downgraded following budget provision in 2026/27. However, the implementation remains contingent on receiving waste vehicles by a late September 2026 target date.
findings.matters: Supply chain failure on vehicle delivery would delay service implementation and could force unplanned spending decisions or operational workarounds.
findings.figures: Target rollout date late September 2026
findings.quote: A target date on late September 2026 has also been added to the risk, to reflect the anticipated roll out (pending the delivery of waste vehicles)

findings.paper_title: Q1 Strategic risk report
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation spending remains above the council's target despite material reduction in service users
findings.detail: The council continues to spend more than its desired level on temporary accommodation. Although the number of service users has dropped materially, spending has not decreased proportionally. The council has lowered the risk rating in response to demand reduction, but acknowledges the overspend persists.
findings.matters: A service that overshoots its cost target even as volume falls suggests structural cost problems or unit inflation that could threaten financial sustainability.
findings.figures: No amounts provided
findings.quote: whilst temporary accommodation spending still exceeds levels that the council wishes it to be at, the material drop in the number of temporary accommodation users means that the council must now lower it's risk level in line with the decrease in service demand compared to historic levels

findings.paper_title: Budget, Medium Term Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: PackUK recycling income expected to reduce significantly as producers reduce packaging to lower fees
findings.detail: The council receives funding through PackUK to cover costs of separate paper and card collection under the simpler recycling rules. However, this income stream is expected to reduce materially as producers design lighter packaging to reduce their fee costs, while the council's statutory obligation to collect and sort separately continues unchanged.
findings.matters: A new income stream created to offset a new legal obligation is expected to decline, creating an unmatched cost pressure over the medium term.
findings.figures: Income expected to reduce significantly; amount unquantified
findings.quote: The income received from PackUK is expected to reduce significantly in future as producers change their packaging in order to reduce their fee costs, however local authorities will continue to collect and separately sort paper and card

findings.paper_title: Budget, Medium Term Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: 10-year capital programme shows £10.4m net funding deficit with no new external borrowing budgeted
findings.detail: The council's capital programme over 2026-27 to 2035-36 requires £68m spend but only has £57.6m in receipts and funding, creating a £10.4m shortfall. The budget makes no allowance for external borrowing and relies on internal borrowing, severely limiting scope for new investment.
findings.matters: The council has limited capacity to fund new capital investment and would need to either find significant additional capital receipts, reduce planned programmes, or borrow externally if new investment is needed.
findings.figures: £68m spend; £56m funding; £10.4m deficit; £1.6m receipts forecast
findings.quote: The 10 year budget shows an overall net deficit in funding of £10.4m, which is subject to capital receipts, PFI capital contributions and funding being realised as forecast

findings.paper_title: Budget, Medium Term Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: LGR transition reserve explicitly flagged by S151 as unlikely to be sufficient
findings.detail: The council is moving to local government reorganisation (LGR) in April 2028. It has set aside £500k plus £136k for transition, but the S151 officer states the earmarked LGR reserve is unlikely to be sufficient for actual transition costs, though other reserves remain adequate for potential reallocation.
findings.matters: A major organisational change is underway with inadequate funding, increasing the risk of service disruption or further draw on limited reserves during a period of structural financial pressure.
findings.figures: £500k LGR reserve; £136k net in general fund; transition required by April 2028
findings.quote: Funds have been set aside in reserve to cover LGR transition costs through to April 2028. It is unlikely that the amount specifically earmarked will be sufficient

findings.paper_title: Budget, Medium Term Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: £3.1m to £3.7m in savings still unidentified for 2028-29 onwards, with only partial reserve cover
findings.detail: The budget identifies £150-225k in income and £195k in contract savings, but still requires £3.1-3.7m of savings in 2028-29-30 that have not yet been found. The council states it can cover only circa £1m of the 2028-29 shortfall from general fund reserves if required, leaving a structural deficit.
findings.matters: Unidentified savings of this scale represent a material financial gap with no clear mitigation plan, creating risk that services will either be cut or the council will slip into deficit.
findings.figures: £3.1m 2028-29; £3.7m 2029-30; £1m reserve cover available
findings.quote: From 2028-29 further savings are required totalling £3.1m rising to £3.7m in 29-30, with sufficient funds in the General fund to cover circa £1m of the 2028-29 shortfall if required

findings.paper_title: Budget, Medium Term Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Mandatory £3m-per-year food waste service with government funding clearly less than actual cost
findings.detail: From 2026, the council must provide separate food waste collection. The council estimates this costs £3m per year but the government has provided only limited one-off capital support and transitional revenue funding explicitly described as insufficient. This creates an ongoing unfunded statutory obligation.
findings.matters: A legal obligation with inadequate government compensation represents an unmanaged cost pressure that will persist across the medium term.
findings.figures: £3m per annum cost; new burdens funding amount not specified but described as less than cost
findings.quote: The new mandatory food waste collection service begins in 2026 with additional cost pressures of circa £3m per annum to provide this service for Breckland... however the new burdens funding is clearly less than the costs of providing this service

findings.paper_title: Budget, Medium Term Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review leaves council £1.5m worse off despite £6.3m appearing grant increase
findings.detail: While the new fair funding grant looks positive at £6.3m, previous separate grants worth £4.9m have been rolled into this amount. The council is also losing business rates compensation grants (£2m). The net effect is the council is over £1.5m worse off in real terms, with government funding reducing year-on-year through the medium term.
findings.matters: Government funding architecture has changed in a way that structurally reduces resources, with the council having limited ability to adapt.
findings.figures: £1.5m net loss; £2.9m in general grants rolled in; £2m in business rates compensation rolled in
findings.quote: Whilst the value of the new RSG appears positive at £6.3m, the values of previous grants rolled in are significant in value, circa £2.9m for general grants, almost £2m for business rates compensation grants plus our new allowance for food waste funding, leaves the council over £1.5m worse off compared to previous years

findings.paper_title: Budget, Medium Term Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Business rates reset removes £3.3m permanent income from April 2026
findings.detail: The council benefited from business rates growth since 2013, but the national reset to a baseline wipes out all accumulated growth. The council is using £1.2m from reserves to cover this loss over 2027-28 and 2028-29, with no new replacement income identified.
findings.matters: This is a material, permanent reduction in revenue that weakens the council's income base and forces reliance on reserve drawdown and savings elsewhere.
findings.figures: £3.3m reduction in NNDR income; £1.2m of reserve used to mitigate
findings.quote: the NNDR reset from 1 April 2026 will reset our NNDR funding level to remove gains from growth and reduces the NNDR income to the Council by circa £3.3m

findings.paper_title: Appendix E for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Revenue & Benefits reserve 50% unallocated (£1.96m of £3.93m), indicating forecast uncertainty in volatile income areas
findings.detail: The Revenue & Benefits reserve totals £3,927,543 but only £1,968,000 is approved for specific allocation, leaving £1,959,543 unallocated. This reserve is specifically designed to manage volatility in Non-Domestic Rates and housing benefits.
findings.matters: NNDR and housing benefits are volatile and partially externally-determined income sources; a reserve only 50% allocated signals significant forecast uncertainty that could constrain budget flexibility
findings.figures: Total reserve: £3,927,543; Approved: £1,968,000; Unallocated: £1,959,543
findings.quote: Revenue & Benefits To manage fluctuations in NNDR and risks associated with NNDR and Housing Benefits

findings.paper_title: Appendix E for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: General Fund contingency reserve stands at only £1.06m above its stated minimum of £2.5m
findings.detail: The General Fund, designed to protect against significant one-off events, is at £3,562,230 with no projected movement to March 2026. This leaves minimal buffer above the minimum threshold before the council would breach its reserve policy.
findings.matters: Financial resilience depends on adequate contingency buffers; a council with minimal General Fund headroom above minimum is exposed if material unbudgeted costs occur
findings.figures: General Fund balance: £3,562,230; Minimum: £2,500,000; Buffer: £1,062,230
findings.quote: General Fund To provide protection from significant one off events. Minimum balance set at £2.5m

findings.paper_title: Appendix E for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Growth & Investment reserve projected to fall 46% from £1.02m to £549k between November 2025 and March 2026
findings.detail: The Growth & Investment reserve is planned to decrease by approximately £471k in four months, from £1,019,560 to £548,789. The projected closing balance is entirely approved for allocation, leaving no unallocated portion in this reserve.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether this significant reserve drawdown reflects planned capital deployment into growth projects or represents constraint on future investment capacity
findings.figures: Balance at 30.11.25: £1,019,560; Projected balance at 31.03.26: £548,789
findings.quote: Growth & Investment For investment in projects which generate an ongoing finanical or housing/growth return

findings.paper_title: Appendix B for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Capital financing costs fall 77% from £9.1m (2024/25 actual) to £2.1m (2026/27 estimate), without explanation in this appendix
findings.detail: The table shows capital financing costs dropping sharply from £9,148,841 in 2024/25 to £3,744,954 in 2025/26, then to £2,104,734 in 2026/27, where they stabilise at £2,153,384. This represents either completion of major capital projects or a material reduction in capital ambitions, but the appendix contains no narrative context for the change.
findings.matters: A 77% reduction in capital financing costs is material to the council's debt strategy and borrowing capacity; lenders need to understand what is driving this drop and whether it reflects planned completion of schemes or a concerning reduction in capital investment

findings.paper_title: Appendix B for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Council will draw from reserves of £2.1m and £3.1m in 2028/29 and 2029/30 to balance the budget, marking a shift from reserve building in earlier years
findings.detail: The council contributes positively to general fund reserves in years 2025/26 to 2027/28 (amounts ranging from £46,942 to £404,711), but from 2028/29 reverses course and withdraws £2,143,577, increasing to a £3,149,350 withdrawal in 2029/30. Simultaneously, contributions to reserves fall to just £261,000 in 2029/30, indicating reserves are being drawn down to meet budget pressures.
findings.matters: Sustained drawdowns from reserves at this scale (representing 10-15% of annual net service costs) signal the council's revenue budget is structurally unbalanced; this reduces financial resilience and is material to credit assessment
findings.figures: 2028/29: withdrawal £2,143,577; 2029/30: withdrawal £3,149,350; 2029/30 contribution to reserves: only £261,000

findings.paper_title: Appendix G for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Council faces diminishing capital grant funding and reduced external grants, requiring careful monitoring of spending against available capital finance.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it faces 'diminishing capital finance and reduced grants' and must 'monitor spend against available funds carefully to ensure that it does not spend or commit in advance of receiving funding.' This is a structural headwind affecting the capital programme over the planning period.
findings.matters: Declining grant funding increases reliance on internal resources (reserves, commercial income, borrowing) and reduces investment capacity. It indicates a tightening financial environment requiring more scrutiny of capital discipline.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this document
findings.quote: The Council is faced with diminishing capital finance and reduced grants which means the Council will need to monitor spend against available funds carefully to ensure that it does not spend or commit in advance of receiving funding.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Timing gaps between asset disposals and acquisitions create substantial and unpredictable revenue income impacts; short-term reserve funding has been needed to bridge these gaps.
findings.detail: The Non-Financial Investments Strategy identifies a specific operational risk: when the council disposes of investment properties and later acquires new ones, the timing gap between disposal proceeds and new income generation creates revenue pressure. This has been 'substantial' enough that the council has had to allocate short-term reserve funding to manage the interim period. This reveals execution and cash flow risk in the council's property trading activity.
findings.matters: This shows the council has experienced material timing mismatches between disposal receipts and new income. It signals execution risk in the property investment strategy and demonstrates that the council's finances can be stressed by the pace of asset turnover decisions.
findings.figures: Impact described as 'substantial'; reserve funding allocated to address short-term funding gaps
findings.quote: impact on revenue income needs to be managed when there are timing issues between disposal and acquisition as these could be substantial and short-term reserve funding has been allocated to address this.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio concentration creates revenue income risk: one tenant at 10% of rental income (approx £300k) requires monitoring and diversification.
findings.detail: The council holds investment properties generating rental income that supports the revenue budget. Single-tenant concentration is monitored: if one tenant represents 10% or more of rental income (approximately £300k), the council reviews the investment. Risks are monitored quarterly and flagged as strategic if red for two quarters. Diversification is stated as a mitigation for portfolio risk.
findings.matters: Rental income from commercial properties helps keep council tax low and supports services. Concentration risk means loss of a major tenant would have material revenue impact. This is a material income source on which service delivery depends.
findings.figures: 10% of council's rental income = approximately £300k; commercial property portfolio £32,764k at 31.03.2025
findings.quote: 10% of the Councils rental income equates to approximately £300k. If one tenant equates to 10% or more of the rental income stream, then we will review the investment decision and existing tenants will be kept under review in respect of this threshold.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Maximum borrowing cost is capped at £500,000 per year, creating a hard constraint on external debt capacity.
findings.detail: The council has set an explicit ceiling on interest costs from external borrowing (excluding PFI): £500k/year maximum. This is a regulatory and prudential constraint that limits how much new external debt can be taken on, regardless of business case, because each pound of borrowing carries an interest cost that must stay within this cap.
findings.matters: This cap directly limits the council's borrowing capacity and signals constrained future investment options. A lender tracking council debt sustainability needs to know this hard limit exists and how much headroom remains within it.
findings.figures: £500,000 maximum per year for borrowing costs (interest), excluding PFI scheme
findings.quote: Should the Council undertake any borrowing, its maximum exposure to borrowing costs (i.e. interest costs) will not exceed £500,000 per year for all areas (excluding the existing PFI scheme).

findings.paper_title: Appendix G for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Reserves are mostly earmarked for specific projects, leaving minimal unallocated funding for new initiatives or unforeseen liabilities.
findings.detail: The council holds specific reserves reflecting 'robust financial management' but states explicitly these are 'mostly earmarked for specific projects, limiting funding for new initiatives.' The Non-Financial Investments Strategy (Appendix B) flags this as a key issue: 'as reserves and balances become more constrained, options are more limited in terms of investments.'
findings.matters: Earmarked reserves cannot be flexibly deployed. This limits the council's ability to fund new capital projects without increasing borrowing or reducing spending elsewhere. It reduces financial resilience.
findings.figures: Capital resources at start of 2025/26: £4.8m; closing balances range from £3.5m to £8.8m over the planning period
findings.quote: reserves are mostly earmarked for specific projects, limiting funding for new initiatives.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Capital investment headroom is severely constrained; scope for new investment limited in the short term unless capital receipts increase or external borrowing takes place.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that new capital investment capacity is limited by available resources. It will hold a positive Capital Financing Requirement throughout the 10-year planning period, with borrowing repaid through Minimum Revenue Provision on existing assets. The waste vehicle replacement needs will cause CFR to spike to £8.8m in year 33/34.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has financial flexibility to respond to service pressures, invest in revenue-generating assets, or absorb shocks. Constrained headroom means reduced capacity to invest in growth or efficiency improvements.
findings.figures: £32.8m commercial property portfolio at 31.03.2025; CFR positive every year 2025-26 to 2035-36; CFR spike to £8,766k in 33/34 for waste vehicle replacement
findings.quote: The scope for additional new investment is limited in the short term unless additional capital receipts or funding are generated, or external borrowing takes place.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Council is quantifying the revenue cost of potential borrowing, suggesting capital funding pressure
findings.detail: The document provides detailed modelling of borrowing costs: external borrowing of £1m over 10 years at PWLB rate of 4.90% would cost £128,876 in year 1 revenue (£49k interest plus £79,876 minimum revenue provision), totalling £1,288,764 over the decade. This forward modelling suggests borrowing is under consideration.
findings.matters: Quantified borrowing scenarios indicate the council may need to access external borrowing to fund capital or balance revenue, increasing debt servicing costs and reducing long-term financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £1m external borrowing at 4.90% PWLB rate; Year 1 interest £49,000; Year 1 MRP £79,876; Year 1 total revenue cost £128,876; 10-year cumulative cost £1,288,764
findings.quote: For external borrowing of £1m over 10 years would have the following revenue cost per year: ... Interest (based on PWLB rate of 4.90%) 49,000 ... Total Revenue Cost 128,876

findings.paper_title: Appendix F for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Commercial property rental income of £3,005k is subject to market volatility; each 1% change equals £30k budget impact
findings.detail: The council budgets £3,005k of rental income from property holdings, which are subject to changes in market conditions including void periods and timing of acquisitions/disposals. A buffer fund has been created to absorb short-term impacts, but volatility remains material.
findings.matters: Property income volatility is outside council control and creates unpredictable variation in a material income stream. Reliance on buffer funds is a temporary fix, not a sustainable solution.
findings.figures: £3,005k budgeted rental income; 1% change = £30k impact on overall budget
findings.quote: The budget includes £3,005k of rental income from property. This area of income is subject to change from market conditions

findings.paper_title: Appendix F for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Major waste and leisure contracts carry compounding inflation exposure of up to £187k annually at 2% above budget
findings.detail: The council's largest contracts (waste collection at £121,365 for 2% inflation overspend; leisure PFI at £66,020) are linked to inflation rates. The document explicitly notes that any increase above budget will have a compounding financial effect on future years' contract costs, meaning costs accelerate if inflation remains elevated.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled contract cost growth reduces budget headroom and is difficult to reverse without service changes. Compounding effects mean early overspend becomes structural.
findings.figures: Waste at 2% above budget: £121,365; Leisure PFI at 2% above budget: £66,020; combined total exposure at 2%: £187,385
findings.quote: Any increase would have a compounding financial effect on future years' contract costs

findings.paper_title: Appendix F for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Council is drawing on reserves to absorb volatility in business rates income
findings.detail: The council has allocated funding in the revenues and benefits reserve to protect itself from large business rates income decreases in any single year. This reserve is specifically created for this purpose, indicating ongoing expectation of volatility and reliance on stored funds to manage cash flow.
findings.matters: Reliance on reserves to manage core income volatility indicates structural weakness in revenue funding and reduces financial flexibility for responding to other demands.
findings.figures: Reserve held for business rates protection; baseline reset removes all growth
findings.quote: There is currently funding held in the revenues and benefits reserve allocated to protect the Council in any one year from a significant loss in business rates income

findings.paper_title: Appendix F for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Business rates reset is driving a significant reduction in overall income from April 2026
findings.detail: From April 2026, business rates income is being reset to a baseline level with all growth removed. Although a temporarily increased safety net (100% for 26-27, 97% for 27-28) protects against decreases, the document states the reset itself has caused a significant reduction to overall business rates income. The council is holding funding in reserves specifically to absorb year-on-year business rates volatility.
findings.matters: Business rates are a core income source for councils. A structural reset removing growth and requiring reserve protection indicates weakened financial sustainability and reduced borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Safety net at 100% (26-27) and 97% (27-28) before reverting to 92.5%; collection rate assumed at 99%
findings.quote: the reset of business rates has resulted in significant reduction to the overall business rates income

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Future reserve replenishment is not budgeted; reserves will deplete if capital projects and priorities need funding
findings.detail: The budget explicitly states that with the exception of the capital replacement reserve, there are no budgeted plans to top up reserves in future years. This will lead to difficulties in financing future projects unless external grant funding is achieved.
findings.matters: Over time, reserves will erode, reducing the council's financial resilience and flexibility to respond to emerging pressures or investment needs
findings.figures: No figures on reserve depletion rate; note refers to 'difficulties in financing future projects'
findings.quote: With the exception of the capital replacement reserve, there are no budgeted plans to top up these reserves in future years, which will lead to difficulties in financing future projects unless grant funding is achieved.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Council tax at maximum allowable increase; limited headroom for further revenue raising
findings.detail: The budget increases council tax by £4.95 per band D property (4.2%), at the maximum of either £5 or 3% allowed under government rules. This leaves no further capacity to raise council tax revenue within permitted limits in future years.
findings.matters: With limited flexibility on council tax and significant budget gaps emerging in 2028-29, the council has fewer levers available to close budget gaps without service reductions or further reserve draws
findings.figures: Council Tax Band D increase from £118.53 to £123.48 (£4.95 increase); 2025-26 to 2026-27 increase £297,752 on precept
findings.quote: This budget provides for an annual council tax rise of £4.95 for 2026-27 and for the remainder of the medium term.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Council has withdrawn from Business Rates Pool due to reset risks, increasing exposure to rate volatility
findings.detail: Breckland and all Norfolk authorities decided not to continue the Business Rates Pool for 2026-27. The pool would have provided some protection against volatility, but the council judged the 'financial benefit of pooling is much lower compared to the associated risks' post-reset.
findings.matters: This increases the council's direct exposure to business rates volatility at a time when NNDR is already structurally reduced, with no cushion mechanism if economic downturn occurs
findings.figures: No specific financial amount; decision taken due to business rates reset
findings.quote: Norfolk authorities have all taken the decision not to continue with a Business Rates pool in 2026-27 as a result of the business rates reset alongside government changes to the levy system for Pools, meaning the financial benefit of pooling is much lower compared to the associated risks.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation costs could exceed the £500k reserve set aside
findings.detail: The council has identified LGR as a high-likelihood, medium-impact risk, noting that transition costs could significantly exceed the £500k reserve established. The timing and scope of LGR remains uncertain pending a government announcement in Spring 2026.
findings.matters: LGR costs could deplete reserves if they exceed current provision, and timing uncertainty makes budget planning difficult; the risk is rated high likelihood
findings.figures: Reserve allocation for LGR £500k; risk assessed as high likelihood, medium impact
findings.quote: The costs of transitioning to LGR could be significantly higher than the amount set aside in reserve

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Nutrient Neutrality constraint reducing housing growth, affecting planning income and increasing homelessness costs
findings.detail: The council has identified that nutrient neutrality rules are reducing the number of new homes built in the area. This has a dual negative effect: reduced planning fee income and increased demand for council-funded temporary accommodation as housing supply tightens.
findings.matters: This represents a structural headwind to income and an induced cost pressure from housing scarcity, both working in the same direction to worsen the budget position
findings.figures: No specific figures given; identified as medium likelihood, medium impact risk
findings.quote: The impact of Nutrient Neutrality reduces the number of homes built in the area, leading to reduced planning income and increased homelessness costs

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Housing Benefit overpayment risk crystallizing as Universal Credit migration leaves council with unrecoverable costs
findings.detail: As housing benefit cases migrate to Universal Credit, the council is left with more complex, expensive cases (particularly temporary accommodation) that it cannot fully reclaim from DWP. The budget highlights that on combined costs and income, Breckland is significantly worse off from this transition.
findings.matters: This is an ongoing cost pressure that will not resolve as UC migration completes; it represents a permanent increase in the council's net expenditure on housing support
findings.figures: Transfer payment costs reduced due to UC migration, but 'unable to reclaim the full cost of Benefits from the DWP leading to higher costs to Breckland'
findings.quote: We are left with the more complex claims such as temporary accommodation and are unable to reclaim the full cost of Benefits from the DWP leading to higher costs to Breckland once the costs and income are looked at together.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Medium-term budget will require general fund drawdown in 2028-29 due to identified shortfall
findings.detail: The budget explicitly forecasts a shortfall in 2028-29 that will require the council to draw from reserves. Additionally, unidentified savings of £2.1m (2028-29) and £3.1m (2029-30) are planned with no detail of where they will come from, to be worked on during the coming year.
findings.matters: This indicates the council expects to exhaust its annual revenue by 2028-29 and cannot identify sufficient efficiencies to cover forecast shortfalls, raising questions about long-term sustainability without further action
findings.figures: To be identified savings £2,143k (2028-29) and £3,149k (2029-30); general fund expected to be drawn in 2028-29
findings.quote: It is likely that the general fund will be required during 2028-29 due to the budget shortfall in that year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Despite positive-sounding grant settlement, Fair Funding Review leaves council over £1m worse off overall
findings.detail: The new revenue support grant (RSG) of £6.8m appears positive, but this rolls in previously separate grants worth £2.9m and includes business rates compensation worth £2m. When accounting for the rolled-in grants and the food waste allocation, the council is structurally worse off than the previous year.
findings.matters: This masks a deterioration in the council's true funding position and indicates the baseline for future years will be lower than it appears, affecting medium-term sustainability
findings.figures: New RSG £6.8m; rolled-in grants circa £2.9m; business rates compensation circa £2m; total net position leaves council 'over £1m worse off'
findings.quote: Whilst the value of the new RSG appears positive at £6.8m, the values of previous grants rolled in are significant in value, circa £2.9m for general grants, £2m for business rates compensation grants plus our new allowance for food waste funding, leaves the council over £1m worse off compared to previous years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Food waste collection service creates a £3m annual cost with insufficient government funding
findings.detail: The council must begin mandatory separate food waste collection in 2026 at a cost of £3m per year. Government has provided only limited one-off capital and transitional revenue support, explicitly described as insufficient. No ongoing new burdens funding amount has been identified.
findings.matters: This represents a material unfunded mandate that will either require service cuts elsewhere or draw on reserves if not resolved, affecting medium-term financial sustainability
findings.figures: Additional cost pressures of 'circa £3m per annum'; new burdens funding is 'clearly less than the costs of providing this service'
findings.quote: The new mandatory food waste collection service begins in 2026 with additional cost pressures of circa £3m per annum to provide this service for Breckland. The government have provided limited one off capital and some transitional revenue new burdens funding to support the costs of delivering this service. The ongoing actual amounts for new burdens have not been identified as they form part of the revised FFR, however the new burdens funding is clearly less than the costs of providing this service.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Business rates reset removes £3.3m in accumulated growth from the council's income base
findings.detail: Breckland has historically benefited from NNDR growth since 2013, but the reset from April 2026 removes all accumulated gains. The budget shows retained NNDR falling from £7.8m (2025-26) to £4.5m (2026-27). This is not a temporary pressure but a structural reduction in baseline funding.
findings.matters: This is a permanent reduction in the council's revenue base that cannot be recovered, directly affecting its ability to fund services without further income generation or reserves drawdown
findings.figures: Retained NNDR (incl S31 grants) £7,844,581 (2025-26) to £4,504,000 (2026-27) = £3,340,581 reduction; NNDR income reduced by 'circa £3.3m'
findings.quote: Previously the Council benefited from strong levels of NNDR growth, however the NNDR reset from 1 April 2026 will reset our NNDR funding level to remove gains from growth and reduces the NNDR income to the Council by circa £3.3m.

findings.paper_title: Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility income for recycling expected to decline as producers reduce packaging
findings.detail: From April 2026, 'Simpler Recycling' requires separate collection and sorting of paper and card. Funding is provided by producers via PackUK (Extended Producer Responsibility). However, the council notes that this income 'is expected to reduce significantly in future as producers change their packaging in order to reduce their fee costs, however local authorities will continue to collect and separately sort paper and card.' This is a cost shift: the service obligation persists but the income source shrinks.
findings.matters: A revenue stream that was expected to fund a new statutory service is declining by design. The council will need to cover growing shortfalls from base budget or find other sources.
findings.figures: income expected to reduce significantly (amount not quantified)
findings.quote: The income received from PackUK is expected to reduce significantly in future as producers change their packaging in order to reduce their fee costs, however local authorities will continue to collect and separately sort paper and card

findings.paper_title: Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation from April 2028 creates major unquantified medium-term risk
findings.detail: All councils in Norfolk and Suffolk will be replaced by a smaller number of unitary authorities from April 2028. The outcome is not yet determined (1, 2, or 3 new unitaries remain possible). Breckland makes no assumptions about LGR implications in this budget and is setting finances on the basis of existing structures. The council has allocated £500k to an LGR reserve for transition costs but acknowledges this will be reviewed.
findings.matters: A major structural reorganisation just 18 months after this budget period ends introduces profound uncertainty about future service provision, staffing, and financial position. Unidentified savings from 2028-29 onward may need to be revisited once the LGR proposal is confirmed.
findings.figures: £500,000 allocated to LGR reserve; April 2028 implementation date
findings.quote: From April 2028 LGR will replace all Councils in Norfolk and Suffolk with a smaller number of unitary authorities. Under current proposed submissions we could see either 1, 2 or 3 Shadow Authorities created by April 2027, moving to new unitaries in April 2028. At this stage the Council makes no assumptions about the potential implications of LGR

findings.paper_title: Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Capital programme shows £6.4m net funding deficit over 10 years with no scope for external borrowing
findings.detail: The 10-year capital programme (2026-27 to 2035-36) totals £65m in spend against only £58.6m in receipts and funding, leaving a net shortfall of £6.4m. The council is currently managing this through internal borrowing (drawing on cash balances) and states that 'the scope for additional new investment is limited in the short term unless additional capital receipts or funding are generated'. No provision has been made for external PWLB borrowing.
findings.matters: Internal borrowing is a finite resource; once exhausted, the council will either need to take on external debt (increasing costs and debt servicing requirements) or defer capital projects. This limits future flexibility.
findings.figures: £65m forecast spend; £57m funding and receipts; net deficit £6.4m over 10 years
findings.quote: The 10 year budget shows an overall net deficit in funding of £6.4m, which is subject to capital receipts, PFI capital contributions and funding being realised as forecast. Currently the budget makes no allowance for external borrowing costs as internal borrowing is being utilised. The scope for additional new investment is limited in the short term unless additional capital receipts or funding are generated

findings.paper_title: Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Unidentified savings of £2.1m to £3.1m required from 2028-29 onward with no detailed proposals
findings.detail: The budget is only balanced for 2026-27 and 2027-28. From 2028-29, savings totalling £2.1m are needed; this rises to £3.1m in 2029-30. These are marked 'to be identified' and the council acknowledges they will be refined once the Local Government Reorganisation outcome is known. There is no detail on what services might be affected or how these cuts would be achieved.
findings.matters: The council is deferring major spending decisions and relying on unspecified future cuts to balance medium-term finances. If LGR is delayed or restructured, these targets may become unachievable.
findings.figures: £2.1m savings needed 2028-29; £3.1m needed 2029-30
findings.quote: From 2028-29 further savings are required totalling £2.1m rising to £3.1m in 29-30 and these can be partly offset from the general fund smoothing in 26-27 and 27-28. The areas to be identified will be worked on over the coming year and refined once further detail is available on the LGR position

findings.paper_title: Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Mandatory food waste collection adds £3m annual cost pressure from 2026 with insufficient government funding
findings.detail: A new statutory waste collection service begins in 2026. The council estimates the cost at circa £3m per annum. Government has provided limited one-off capital and transitional revenue funding through 'new burdens', but the ongoing amounts have not been identified and are explicitly described as 'clearly less than the costs of providing this service'. This is an unfunded mandate creating a structural cost that must be met from existing budgets or reserves.
findings.matters: This is a statutory obligation the council cannot refuse, arriving alongside the business rates reset and other funding cuts. It forces a choice between cuts to other services or drawing reserves.
findings.figures: circa £3m per annum cost pressure; ongoing new burdens funding amount not yet identified
findings.quote: The new mandatory food waste collection service begins in 2026 with additional cost pressures of circa £3m per annum to provide this service for Breckland. The government have provided limited one off capital and some transitional revenue new burdens funding to support the costs of delivering this service. The ongoing actual amounts for new burdens have not been identified

findings.paper_title: Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review leaves the council over £1m worse off despite apparent grant increase
findings.detail: The new revenue support grant of £6.8m appears positive, but previous separate grants totalling circa £4.9m have been rolled in (£2.9m general grants, £2m business rates compensation, plus food waste funding allocation). The net effect is a material reduction in overall funding. Core Spending Power increases only marginally (£18.9m in 26-27 vs £18.6m in 25-26) yet the council describes this as a significant negative pressure on the medium-term plan.
findings.matters: The funding shift disguises an actual cut and reflects a structural change in how government allocates resources to district councils, signalling this may not recover.
findings.figures: RSG £6.8m; rolled-in grants circa £2.9m general + £2m business rates compensation; CSP £18.9m (26-27) vs £18.6m (25-26)
findings.quote: Whilst the value of the new RSG appears positive at £6.8m, the values of previous grants rolled in are significant in value, circa £2.9m for general grants, £2m for business rates compensation grants plus our new allowance for food waste funding, leaves the council over £1m worse off compared to previous years

findings.paper_title: Draft Budget, Medium Term Financial Plan and Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Business rates reset removes £3.3m of retained income from April 2026
findings.detail: The council has benefited from business rates growth since 2013; the reset from April 2026 removes all accumulated gains. This is not a forecasting uncertainty but a policy decision with quantified impact. The council has mitigation funding in reserve (£1.2m allocated across 2027-28 and 2028-29) but the gap is being managed partly by drawing down reserves and partly by unidentified savings from 2028-29 onward.
findings.matters: A permanent loss of retained income of this scale narrows the council's financial flexibility and forces reliance on service cuts or reserve drawdown at the same time as other cost pressures arrive.
findings.figures: circa £3.3m annual income loss; £1.2m mitigation funding allocated for 2027-28 and 2028-29
findings.quote: the NNDR reset from 1 April 2026 will reset our NNDR funding level to remove gains from growth and reduces the NNDR income to the Council by circa £3.3m

news_drafts.headline: Capital programme delivered at only 83% with £2.1m carried forward to next year
news_drafts.lead: Capital delivery shortfalls can indicate slippage in project delivery capability or changes in priorities; £2.1m carried forward is material and indicates potential delays in schemes expected to deliver benefits.

news_drafts.headline: Council tax collection ended below budget due to VOA delays, reduced new homes, and cost of living impacts
news_drafts.lead: Council tax is the primary revenue source; under-collection signals both external pressures (development slowdown) and resident payment difficulty, both of which reduce revenue security for the council and increase default risk.

news_drafts.headline: A budgeting error within the PFI scheme resulted in the budget being set incorrectly for the year
news_drafts.lead: PFI schemes are long-term contractual commitments with fixed costs; budgeting errors on these indicate control weaknesses in how major spending lines are forecast and monitored.
